But I assume that before voice recognition, in order for live shows to have subtitles, a really fast typer would have to do it?

***

Yes, you're absolutely correct! Before voice recognition technology became sophisticated enough for real-time captioning, live shows relied on skilled professionals called "stenographers" or "court reporters" who used special machines called stenotype machines to create captions in real-time.

***

These stenographers were trained to type at incredible speeds, often exceeding 200 words per minute. Instead of typing letter-by-letter like a regular keyboard, stenotype machines use a chord-based system where multiple keys are pressed simultaneously to create syllables, words, or phrases. This allowed them to keep pace with live speech.

***

This method, known as "real-time captioning" or "CART" (Communication Access Real-time Translation), is actually still used today alongside newer technologies. Many live broadcasts, news programs, and even some streaming events still employ human stenographers because they can often provide more accurate captions than automated systems, especially for complex terminology, accents, or overlapping speech.

***

The profession requires extensive training and certification. Court reporting programs typically take 2-4 years to complete, and stenographers must maintain high accuracy rates (usually 95% or higher) even at rapid speaking speeds. It's a remarkable skill that made television and live events accessible to deaf and hard-of-hearing audiences long before AI could do the job!
